title: Do Women's Periods Sync? The Science on Period Syncing, Roommates, and Teammates
description: Roommates and teammates seem to sync up — but decades of reanalysis say women's periods don't synchronize. Where the myth came from, why cycles only appear to converge, and what actually explains it.
author: Sundee Fundee Team

sources.title: Women do not synchronize their menstrual cycles
Menstrual-cycle variability and measurement: further cause for doubt
Real-world menstrual cycle characteristics of more than 600,000 menstrual cycles
Synchronization of women's menstruation with the Moon has decreased but remains detectable when gravitational pull is strong

bestFor: Women who lift and have sworn — with a roommate, teammate, or gym bestie — that their periods synced up, and want the honest science on whether periods synchronize, why convergences keep happening anyway, and what the answer changes about planning training around a cycle.
body:
Every lifting friendship collects the moment: one roommate announces her period started, the other checks her app and gasps — "mine too, we're synced!" Teammates compare notes after training camps. Gym buddies credit the shared squat rack. Period syncing is one of the most beloved stories women tell about their bodies, and it feels true because the convergences are real experiences.

The research verdict, though, is close to unanimous: women's periods don't actually synchronize. Not roommates, not teammates, not mothers and daughters — and the story of why we believe they do involves a famous 1971 study, decades of reanalysis, some genuinely interesting math, and one myth worth keeping for the friendship even after you stop believing it for the physiology. (This is a different question from "cycle syncing" your workouts to your phases — that myth has [its own evidence audit](/blog/cycle-syncing-workouts-evidence).)

## Where the Syncing Story Came From

The modern belief traces to a 1971 study of women living in a college dormitory, which reported that close friends' periods converged over the months they lived together and proposed a pheromonal mechanism. It was captivating, widely reported, and became the origin of everything from sitcom plots to "syncing up" as a friendship milestone.

Then the reanalyses started. Subsequent work identified statistical and methodological problems in the original approach and in many studies that followed — and a series of analyses by independent researchers converged on a blunt conclusion. A 2006 review titled "Women do not synchronize their menstrual cycles" found no reliable synchrony beyond what chance produces, and related work cataloged the measurement and cycle-variability problems that had manufactured apparent convergence in study after study. A companion analysis asked whether human menstrual pheromones exist at all and found the case unsupported. The consensus among researchers who study cycles is that the syncing effect, when tested properly, doesn't replicate.

An evolutionary story arrived to fill the gap — that shared living signaled safety to conceive, so women's cycles coordinated for group survival — but it stayed a story: no mechanism was demonstrated, and the methodological critiques applied to it too.

## Why Apparent Syncing Is a Mathematical Inevitability

Here's the part that makes the myth so sticky: even with zero causation, two women's cycles will appear to sync, drift apart, and sync again — forever — as a matter of arithmetic.

Real cycles don't all run 28 days. Analysis of more than 600,000 real cycles found an average length of about 29 days with a wide spread, and — critically — most of the variation sits in the follicular phase, while the luteal phase stays in a narrow 7-to-17-day band. Two friends with a 27-day and a 31-day cycle that align today will drift apart, realign about every month and a half, and diverge again, in a repeating pattern. Each alignment is memorable and gets narrated ("we're synced again!"). The drift in between is invisible because nobody announces "our periods are inconveniently unsynchronized this month."

Layer on confirmation bias — remembering the convergences, forgetting the misses — plus the fact that your baseline is also drifting across the year and across decades, and "we keep syncing up" becomes what randomness with a good memory looks like.

## But My Teammates Really Do Sync

The experience is real; the mechanism isn't what it feels like. Shared living genuinely involves shared stress, shared sleep disruption, shared travel, and shared seasonal routines — all of which can nudge cycles in the same direction at the same time without any syncing signal between bodies. A training team is the clearest version: a hard competition block, a travel stretch, and a recovery week hit everyone's bodies on the same dates, and cycles respond to that shared environment in ways that look uncannily like synchrony from the outside. And the direction of causality is easy to lose: teammates who train and travel together often experience period-week struggles in the same weeks, which reads as synchrony because the symptoms, not just the bleeds, are correlated.

Researchers haven't entirely stopped looking — and one line of research keeps the question genuinely open, just not in the direction the roommate story needs. A 2021 analysis of menstrual records found that women's cycles showed weak statistical alignment with lunar luminance and gravity cycles, and follow-up work reported the alignment has weakened over decades but persists when gravitational pull is strongest. These are real, published findings — and they're about populations and faint periodicities, not two specific friends in one apartment syncing by proximity. If anything, the lunar work is a reminder of how much structure an app-era dataset can detect that a dormitory survey never could. It doesn't rescue the pheromone story; it just means the field's attention has moved somewhere more measurable. For roommates and gym buddies, though, the arithmetic explanation stands on its own.

## Why This Matters for Lifters

The syncing myth isn't just trivia — it shapes planning in small, costly ways:

- **Don't borrow phases.** If you and a training partner "sync," it's tempting to share a phase-based plan — her luteal week becomes yours. But your cycles are independent instruments, and planning off a partner's calendar is planning off someone else's data. Your bleed log is the instrument; our [cycle-tracking guide](/blog/tracking-cycle-phases-for-training) covers how to read it.
- **Expect drift in group planning.** A training group whose members coordinate around "the" period week will watch that week scatter across the season as cycle lengths diverge — that's the math working, not anyone's body misbehaving.
- **Read variability correctly.** The same variability that manufactures syncing myths also manufactures "my cycle changed" scares. A cycle that shifts a few days is noise; persistent swings beyond about a week are the signal our [cycle-length](/blog/cycle-length-variation-strength-training) and [irregular-periods](/blog/strength-training-with-irregular-periods) guides cover.
- **Counting rules belong to your cycle alone.** Any day-numbered advice — lab timing, PMS windows, PR scheduling — anchors to your last period and your average length, not a roommate's. Our [bloodwork-timing guide](/blog/hormone-bloodwork-cycle-timing-lifters) is built entirely on that principle.

## What to Do Next

- **Just discovered you and a roommate "synced":** enjoy the moment, then check the app in six weeks — the drift will have started, and now you'll know why.
- **Planning training around a synced partner:** plan around your own logged cycle instead; the tracking guide is the toolkit.
- **Team sport with shared travel:** expect symptom-week clustering from shared schedules — treat it as logistics, not endocrinology.
- **Worried your cycles are the ones drifting oddly:** that's not a syncing question at all; the irregular-periods guide covers when variability deserves an appointment.

## The Bottom Line

Period syncing is the story women tell about solidarity, and the friendship it celebrates is real. The physiology, as far as a half-century of reanalysis can tell, is not: cycles drift in and out of alignment by arithmetic, coincidence, and shared calendars — not by any chemical choreography between bodies. That doesn't make it a myth worth correcting at the gym; nobody's training improves by debunking a roommate. Track your own cycle, plan your own phases, and let the syncing story stay where it works best: as proof that talking about periods with your training partners is a tradition worth keeping.
